Declaring data and models

Source: vignettes/model-specification.Rmd
model-specification.Rmd

This vignette describes every part of a lexio study: the notation, the declaration of the database, the goals and scenarios, the priorities, the outputs and the numerical behaviour of the method. vignette("lexio") runs a complete example first.

1. Notation

The notation follows Rocha (2026, section 4.2). With n sectors and k satellite accounts:

Symbol Meaning In lexio
Z (n × n) intermediate transactions: row = selling sector, column = buying sector declare_io(Z = ), file Z
x (n) gross output declare_io(x = ), file x
f (n) final demand declare_io(f = ), file f
A = Z x̂⁻¹ technical coefficients (by column) computed from Z, or declare_io(A = )
B = I − A computed, or declare_io(B = ); io$B
E_j (n) level of satellite account j in each sector (toe, jobs, tonnes, …) declare_io(E = list(j = ...)), file E
D = E x̂⁻¹ (k × n) satellite coefficients: account j per unit of output computed from E, or declare_io(D = ); io$D
b_j = D_j x base of account j satellite_base(io)
G = [D; B] ((k + n) × n) the goal matrix build_lp()$G
g (k + n) the goals: k account goals, then n economic goals build_goals(io, model, scenario)
d⁺, d⁻ deviations above and below each goal run$d_plus, run$d_minus
α_h corridor of sector h, a proportion of |g_h| declare_io(corridor = ), or floor = / ceiling =
P_l priority level l define_model(priorities = )
Z_l optimum of level l (not the matrix Z) run$Z, columns Z1 … ZL of the outputs
ECO the economic block: the n rows of B, with goal f by default the goal "ECO" in the priorities

The goals form the system G x + d⁻ − d⁺ = g, with x, d⁺, d⁻ ≥ 0. The decision variables are ordered x_1 ... x_n, d⁺_1 ... d⁺_{k+n}, d⁻_1 ... d⁻_{k+n}.

2. The database

2.1. In R 

io <- declare_io(
  Z = Z, x = x, f = f,                          # or A = A, or B = B, instead of Z
  E = list(GD = E_GD, GC = E_GC, LAB = E_LAB),  # or D = list(...): coefficients instead of levels
  corridor = alpha,                             # optional: corridor, or floor and/or ceiling
  sectors = data.frame(code = codes, name = names)
)

The technical structure. Give exactly one of Z (flows; the package computes A = Z x̂⁻¹ and B = I − A), A or B. The name of the argument tells the package which object it receives.

The satellite accounts. Give exactly one of E (the level of each account in each sector; the package computes D = E x̂⁻¹) or D (the coefficients per unit of output). The names are the names of the accounts. Accepted forms:

  • a named list of vectors (recommended): E = list(GD = E_GD, LAB = E_LAB), one value per sector;
  • a data frame, one column per account and one row per sector (an optional code column matches the rows to the sectors);
  • a matrix: for E, sectors × accounts; for D, accounts × sectors. The other orientation is detected. A square matrix (k = n) is ambiguous and is refused: use a list.

A single vector without a name is refused: write E = list(LAB = my_vector).

The sectors. A data frame with code and name. Without it, the codes come from the names of x or the column names of Z, or are S01, S02, ….

Accounts of the database and accounts of the model. The model uses only the accounts listed in its accounts. A database with six accounts serves models with one, two or six of them.

2.2. The corridor

α_h is a proportion of |g_h|, the goal of the economic row of sector h (by default, the final demand f_h):

Declaration Bound Meaning
corridor = alpha d⁻_h ≤ α_h |g_h| and d⁺_h ≤ α_h |g_h| two-sided corridor
floor = alpha d⁻_h ≤ α_h |g_h|, that is G_h x ≥ g_h − α_h |g_h| only a floor
ceiling = alpha d⁺_h ≤ α_h |g_h|, that is G_h x ≤ g_h + α_h |g_h| only a ceiling
floor = a1, ceiling = a2 both, with different widths floor and ceiling
nothing no bound free model
  • alpha = 0.05 in a sector lets its economic goal deviate by up to 5% of |g_h|.
  • NA in a sector leaves that sector without a bound on that side.
  • corridor together with floor or ceiling is an error.
  • The model multiplies α by corridor: multiplier (default 1) and can switch the corridor off with corridor: use: false, also in a single scenario (section 3.3).
  • If the corridor comes from a quantity per sector (for instance, the purchases of energy by each sector), compute the proportion first: alpha <- purchases / x.
  • The satellite goals never have a corridor.

2.3. Files

read_io(path) reads a folder of CSV files, or an .xlsx workbook with sheets of the same names. write_io(io, dir) writes a declared database in this format, and lexio_template(dir) writes an example database with a commented model.yml.

File / sheet Columns Content
sectors code, name the sectors; sets n and the order of the sectors in the outputs
Z, A or B (one) code + one column per sector (header = codes) the technical structure
x code, value gross output
f code, value final demand
E or D (one) code + one column per account levels or coefficients of the satellite accounts; the headers are the account names
corridor, or floor and/or ceiling (optional) code, alpha proportions α_h (empty or NA = no bound)
  • Codes are text (0191 stays 0191). The rows of each file are matched to the sectors by code, in any order.
  • CSV files may use , as separator and . as decimal mark, or ; and ,. The format is detected from the first line of each file.
  • Z, x and f are in the same currency unit; each satellite account is in its own unit.
  • Write the numbers with all their digits (up to 17 significant digits). write_io() does this. Section 7.2 explains why it matters.

2.4. Checks

declare_io() and read_io() stop with an error when the dimensions are inconsistent, when not exactly one of Z/A/B or of E/D is given, when codes are duplicated or do not match across files, when a value is missing or not finite, when x ≤ 0 in some sector, or when some α is negative. They warn when a column of A sums to 1 or more, when I − A is nearly singular, or when a coefficient is negative. validate_io() gives the full report, including the corridor mode and, whatever the declaration (Z, A or B), the largest discrepancy between (I − A) x and f.

validate_io(example_io())
#>                   check level                                             detail
#> 1            dimensions  info      3 sectors, 3 satellite account(s) (E, I, LAB)
#> 2          columns of A    ok                                 largest sum 0.4375
#> 3                 I - A    ok                         invertible (rcond = 0.497)
#> 4              corridor    ok      two-sided corridor; alpha between 0.1 and 0.2
#> 5 balance (I - A) x = f  info largest |(I - A) x - f| 0 (relative to x 0); sum 0

The economic block uses f as its goal. If f differs from (I − A) x, a run without any shock does not return exactly x: the model closes the gap within the corridor.

3. The model

3.1. A complete model.yml 

name: my_study
data: base                 # the database: a folder (or base.xlsx), relative to this file

accounts:                  # satellite accounts, in declaration order
  GD:
    label: Distributed generation
    unit: toe
    direction: ">="
    target: {type: pooled_share, share: 0.01, pool: [GD, GC]}
  GC:
    label: Centralized generation
    unit: toe
    direction: "<="
    target: {type: base}
  LAB:
    label: Employment
    unit: jobs
    direction: ">="
    target: {type: growth, rate: 0.01}
    weight: 1              # optional; matters only when goals share a level

economy:                   # the economic block ECO (section 3.4)
  direction: ">="
  target: final_demand     # or a list [5, 10, ...] or a CSV file (code, value)
  position: last           # the default: ECO fixed at the last level
  deviation: absolute      # the default; or relative

corridor:                  # the corridor declared with the data
  use: true                # false: free model
  multiplier: 1            # multiplies alpha

scenarios:                 # optional: several sets of goals in the same model
  GD_shock: {}             # the goals in accounts, unchanged
  GC_shock:
    GD: {type: base}
    GC: {type: pooled_share, share: 0.01, pool: [GD, GC]}
  GC_shock_free:
    GD: {type: base}
    GC: {type: pooled_share, share: 0.01, pool: [GD, GC]}
    corridor: {use: false}

priorities: all            # all k! orders, ECO last (section 4)
lock_tolerance: auto       # the default (section 7)

The accepted keys are name, data, accounts, economy, corridor, scenarios, priorities, lock_tolerance and max_orderings. Any other key is an error. read_model() reads the file; run_model("model.yml") reads the model and the database it names.

The same model in R:

pooled <- list(type = "pooled_share", share = 0.01, pool = c("GD", "GC"))
m <- define_model(
  accounts = list(
    GD  = list(direction = ">=", target = pooled, label = "Distributed generation", unit = "toe"),
    GC  = list(direction = "<=", target = list(type = "base"), label = "Centralized generation", unit = "toe"),
    LAB = list(direction = ">=", target = list(type = "growth", rate = 0.01), label = "Employment", unit = "jobs")
  ),
  economy = list(direction = ">=", target = "final_demand"),
  scenarios = list(GD_shock = list(),
                   GC_shock = list(GD = list(type = "base"), GC = pooled)),
  priorities = "all",
  lock_tolerance = "auto"
)

3.2. Directions and goals

Each account has a direction:

Direction Meaning Penalized deviation
">=" floor: do not fall below the goal d⁻
"<=" ceiling: do not exceed the goal d⁺
"=" target: stay on the goal d⁻ and d⁺

and a goal, computed from its base b = D_j x:

target Goal g Typical use
{type: base} b keep the current level
{type: growth, rate: r} b + b·r grow (or shrink, with a negative rate) by a fraction
{type: pooled_share, share: s, pool: [A, B]} b + s·(b_A + b_B) a shock equal to a share of the joint base of a group of accounts
{type: delta, value: v} b + v add an absolute amount
{type: level, value: v} v set an absolute level

The goal g is always the total level of the account, not only the change. For instance, with b_GD = 4.08 and b_GC = 26.18, the goal {type: pooled_share, share: 0.01, pool: [GD, GC]} of GD is 4.08 + 0.01 × (4.08 + 26.18) = 4.38.

io <- example_io()
m <- define_model(list(
  E = list(direction = ">=", target = list(type = "pooled_share", share = 0.05, pool = c("E", "I"))),
  I = list(direction = "<=", target = list(type = "base")),
  LAB = list(direction = ">=", target = list(type = "growth", rate = 0.05))
))
satellite_base(io)
#>     E     I   LAB 
#>   6.6  29.0 260.0
build_goals(io, m)[1:3]
#> [1]   8.38  29.00 273.00

3.3. Scenarios

Each scenario replaces the goals of some accounts, and every scenario runs in every ordering. A scenario may also change:

  • the directions, for example directions: {GC: "=", economy: "="};
  • the corridor, for example corridor: {multiplier: 2} or corridor: {use: false}.

Without scenarios, the model has a single scenario named main.

3.4. The economic block

Goal. By default, the goal of ECO is the declared final demand. In economy: target, a list of values (one per sector) or a CSV file with columns code and value gives another goal; economy: direction changes its direction.

Position. economy: position: last (the default) fixes ECO at the last level: the economic block absorbs the final impact of the goals above it. An ordering may write ECO only as its last level, or omit it; it is added there. To place ECO elsewhere, the model must say so with economy: position: free. Then ECO can be written at any level of an explicit ordering, and with priorities: all (or permute) ECO enters the permutations, giving (k + 1)! orderings. The Miller and Blair example uses this declaration (vignette("miller-blair")).

Deviations. The ECO level minimizes the deviations of the n sectors from their goals.

  • deviation: absolute (the default) adds them in currency units, Σ_h d⁻_h. A shortfall of one currency unit costs the same in every sector, whatever its size.
  • deviation: relative adds them as proportions of each goal, Σ_h d⁻_h / |g_h|. A shortfall of 1% of a sector’s final demand costs the same in every sector.

When the goals above ECO force the economy to give up some final demand, the ECO level chooses which sectors give it up. In the example below, the incumbent energy is cut by 20% at the first level, without a corridor:

io <- example_io()
cut <- list(I = list(direction = "<=", target = list(type = "growth", rate = -0.2)))
for (deviation in c("absolute", "relative")) {
  m <- define_model(cut, economy = list(direction = ">=", target = "final_demand", deviation = deviation),
                    corridor = list(use = FALSE))
  r <- run_experiment(io, m, ordering = 1)
  loss <- r$d_minus[1 + seq_len(io$n)]
  print(data.frame(deviation = deviation, sector = io$sectors$name, loss = round(loss, 2),
                   share_of_demand = round(loss / io$f, 3)))
}
#>   deviation      sector  loss share_of_demand
#> 1  absolute Agriculture  0.00           0.000
#> 2  absolute    Industry 20.45           0.487
#> 3  absolute    Services  0.00           0.000
#>   deviation      sector  loss share_of_demand
#> 1  relative Agriculture 32.14           0.459
#> 2  relative    Industry  0.00           0.000
#> 3  relative    Services  0.00           0.000

With absolute deviations the level chooses the smallest loss in currency, and the loss falls on Industry, where it takes almost half of the demand. With relative deviations it chooses the smallest loss in proportion of each sector’s demand. Each level is a linear program, so the loss is not spread evenly: the solution is a vertex, and it concentrates the loss where it is cheapest in the chosen measure. A corridor already caps the loss of each sector; with a tight corridor the two choices tend to give the same solution. The relative deviations need a nonzero goal g_h in every sector, and the optimum Z of the ECO level is then a sum of proportions.

4. Priorities

Without a declaration, every ordering is run; to run only some orderings, declare them. In every case ECO is the last level, unless the model declares economy: position: free.

4.1. All orders

priorities: all (the default) puts one account per level and runs all k! orders, in the lexicographic order of declaration. With accounts [A, B, C]:

lex_permutations(3)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    2    3
#> [2,]    1    3    2
#> [3,]    2    1    3
#> [4,]    2    3    1
#> [5,]    3    1    2
#> [6,]    3    2    1

The rows are the orderings P01 to P06: A-B-C, A-C-B, B-A-C, B-C-A, C-A-B and C-B-A.

k Levels Orderings per scenario
2 P1, P2, ECO 2
3 P1, P2, P3, ECO 6
4 P1, …, P4, ECO 24
6 P1, …, P6, ECO 720

When the number of orderings exceeds max_orderings (default 720), the package asks for explicit orderings or a higher limit.

4.2. Permuting groups 

priorities:
  permute: [[GD, GC], LAB]   # GD and GC share a level; 2! = 2 orderings, ECO last

Each group is one level with several goals, and every account must be in exactly one group. With economy: position: free, ECO is permuted with the groups.

4.3. Explicit orderings 

priorities:
  first: [LAB, GD, GC]          # one account per level; ECO is added as the last level
  second: [[GD, GC], LAB]       # GD and GC share the first level

In R: priorities = list(first = c("LAB", "GD", "GC"), second = list(c("GD", "GC"), "LAB")). To run a single ordering, list only that one; run_model(..., orderings = ) also runs only some of the orderings of a model.

  • Each account appears exactly once.
  • ECO may be written at the end; elsewhere only with economy: position: free (then [LAB, ECO, [GD, GC]] puts ECO second).
  • ECO is alone in its level.
  • Each goal keeps its own direction, so a level may mix floors and ceilings.

Labels. Unnamed orderings with one account per level and ECO last get the label of their position in the lexicographic order (P05 for C-A-B with k = 3); other unnamed orderings get O01, O02, …; named orderings keep their names.

4.4. Weights

weight (default 1, positive) multiplies the deviation of an account in its level. It matters only when goals share a level: the level minimizes Σ weight × penalized deviation. A level that holds goals in different units adds their deviations, so give them comparable units or weights.

5. Running 

res <- run_model("my_study/model.yml")   # reads the database named in data:
res <- run_model(io, m)                  # or the database and the model already in memory
Argument of run_model() Effect
scenarios only some scenarios (names)
orderings only some orderings (numbers or labels)
strict with TRUE, stops at the first non-optimal level; the default FALSE runs everything and flags it
verbose shows progress
lock_tolerance replaces the setting of the model (section 7)

A single run:

io <- example_io()
m <- read_model(system.file("examples", "toy", "model.yml", package = "lexio"))
r <- run_experiment(io, m, scenario = "I_shock", ordering = c("LAB", "E", "I"))
r$Z        # optimum of each level
#> [1] 0 0 0 0
r$x_star   # output of the last level
#> [1] 100.76394  81.06627  65.85146

ordering can be a number, a label ("P05", "second") or an ordering written as in section 4.3. Each run takes hundredths to tenths of a second: a database with 72 sectors and 6 accounts (720 orderings) runs in about a minute.

6. Outputs

write_outputs(res, dir) writes:

dir/
  README.md            report: model, corridor, ECO, tables per scenario, distinct states, warnings
  results.xlsx         every table in one Excel workbook (see write_excel())
  orderings.csv        one row per scenario × ordering
  levels.csv           one row per scenario × ordering × level: each stage of each run
  level_results.csv    every run, every level, every row of G
  account_goals.csv    one row per scenario × ordering × account
  x_star_all_runs.csv  one row per sector: x0 and the output x* of every run
  states.csv           distinct states (equal x* solutions)
  runs/<scenario>/<label>_<levels>/
                       all_levels.csv, level_1.csv ... level_L.csv, x_star.csv
  inputs/              the model.yml used and the SHA-256 of the database files
  results.rds          the full object (readRDS)
  session.txt          versions of R, of the packages and of GLPK
  • The folder of a run is its label and its levels, for example P04_GC-LAB-GD or book_1_EMP-ECO-OIL+COAL-SO2+HC; ECO is written only when it is not last.
  • format = "intl" (default) writes the CSV files with , and .; format = "br" with ; and ,, for spreadsheets with a comma as decimal mark.
  • An existing folder with files is not overwritten unless overwrite = TRUE.
  • excel = FALSE skips results.xlsx.

orderings.csv (res$summary$runs)

Column Content
scenario, ordering, label, priorities the run and its levels (GD > GC > LAB > ECO)
status GLPK code of each level, concatenated (0000 = all optimal)
status_glpk the same, spelled out (GLP_OPT GLP_OPT GLP_OPT GLP_NOFEAS)
optimal, ok all levels optimal; and, in addition, all checks passed
lock_tolerance lock used in the run (0 = exact; section 7)
corridor corridor mode of the run
Z1 … ZL optimum of each level
delta_x, delta_x_pct change in total gross output, Σ x* − Σ x, and as a fraction
delta_<account> change of each account, D_j x* − b_j
state distinct state of the run

levels.csv (res$summary$levels): one row per level of each run, with its goals, its optimum Z, the GLPK status and the lock used.

level_results.csv: for every run and every level, one row per row of G (row, block = account or ECO), with g, Gx, d_minus, d_plus and, in the ECO rows, the output x of that level.

all_levels.csv (one per run): the same numbers, with the levels side by side: row, notation (xD_j = D_j x; f'_h = row h of (I − A) x), name, block, g, and level<l>_Gx, level<l>_d_minus, level<l>_d_plus and level<l>_x of each level.

account_goals.csv (res$summary$goals)

Column Content
account, unit, direction the account
base, g, Gx base b, goal g and achieved value D_j x*
delta, intended Gx − base and g − base
realized realized share of the intended change, delta / intended
deviation penalized deviation of the account
at_goal the account met its goal

states.csv (res$summary$states). Different orderings may lead to the same solution. Runs whose outputs x* differ by at most 1e-6 in every sector form one state.

results.xlsx: the sheets are described in vignette("lexio") and in ?write_excel.

7. Numerical behaviour

7.1. The lock of the solved levels

Each level locks the previous ones by equality, d_l = Z_l, which holds with zero slack. When the scales of the goals differ widely (toe, jobs and currency units in the same problem), GLPK sometimes declares infeasible (GLP_NOFEAS) a level that has a solution. This is a numerical false infeasibility: another solver (lpSolve) solves the same problem. It depends on the numbers, not on the number of accounts:

Database Runs not optimal with the exact lock
Brazil 2018 (EPE), 72 sectors, k = 3, coefficients with 15 significant digits 0 of 24
the same database at full precision 4 of 24
Brazil 2018 (EPE), k = 4 / 5 / 6 4 of 24 / 20 of 120 / 186 of 720
Brazil 2015 (IBGE), 67 sectors, k = 4 9 of 24

lock_tolerance: auto (the default):

  • every run first uses the exact lock;
  • only if some level is not optimal is the run solved again with the locks relaxed to d_l ≤ Z_l + t·max(1, |Z_l|), with the smallest t among 1e-12, 1e-11, 1e-10 and 1e-9 that makes every level optimal;
  • if no t works, the run keeps the exact lock and is flagged as not optimal.

Runs that are optimal with the exact lock do not change. In the tests with the two real databases, auto made all 906 runs optimal; of the 219 runs solved again, 211 needed only t = 1e-12.

The precision cost. The slack lets each solved level stay above its optimum by up to t·max(1, |Z_l|), and the following levels may use it. In ill-conditioned problems the effect on the following levels is much larger than t: in the tests, t = 1e-9 moved the Z of the following levels by up to about 2e-4 (relative) from an exact solution. Every relaxed run is therefore flagged: run_model() issues a warning, print() shows it, the column lock_tolerance gives the t used and the report lists the runs in its Warnings section. When publishing results, report how many runs needed the relaxed lock.

The other options are lock_tolerance: exact (or 0), which keeps only the exact lock and leaves failing runs flagged as not optimal, and a number t (up to 1e-6), which tries the exact lock and then only t.

7.2. Sensitivity to the last digits

With equality locks, the GLPK status can change under perturbations of the data of the order of 1e-16. The same database written with 15 or with 17 significant digits gives the same numbers up to about 1e-10, but may change the status of borderline runs. For bit-identical results, use bit-identical inputs; write_io() writes the shortest exact decimal representation of each number. On Macs with Apple silicon, R itself may read a number written with 16 or 17 significant digits with a difference in the last bit; numbers with up to 15 significant digits, such as the coefficients of the thesis, are read exactly everywhere.

7.3. Alternative optima

A level may have several optima, with the same Z and a different x. GLPK returns one of them. This is one reason why results are also summarized by distinct states.

7.4. What the model does not impose

  • There is no non-negativity constraint on the satellite accounts (D x) or on the resulting final demand.
  • The corridor applies only to the economic block. The deviations of the satellite accounts are free; their cost lies in the priority order.

7.5. Levels without solution

A level can have no solution: for instance, a zero corridor (α = 0) with an economic goal that no non-negative output meets. GLPK then also reports the level as not optimal. To tell this case from a false infeasibility, lexio checks the solution returned by GLPK against the constraints of the level (goals, corridor, locks and x, d ≥ 0), each row relative to max(1, |right-hand side|):

  • violation up to 1e-4: the constraints hold, so the flag is a false infeasibility; the numbers are kept and the run is flagged as not optimal. In the false infeasibilities we examined (several hundred runs), the violation stayed below 1e-6;
  • violation above 1e-4: the level has no solution. That level and the following ones are left blank (NA) in the run and in every table, the column infeasible_level of summary$runs gives the first one (the report says “no solution from level l”), and the run has no state. In levels without solution the violation is of order 1e-2 or more.

The column violation of summary$levels (and of levels.csv) gives the value for every level. A negative α or corridor multiplier is refused when declared.

8. Scope and limits

  • Size. The matrices are dense. On one laptop, one run with three accounts (four levels) took about 0.1 s with 100 sectors, 0.4 s with 200, 2 s with 400 and 7 s with 600; the times depend on the machine and on the matrix (on another machine, with fully dense random matrices, they were about twice as long), but the time always grows faster than the square of the number of sectors, and a model runs k! orderings per scenario. National tables, with tens to a few hundred sectors, are within reach; multiregional tables with thousands of sectors are not.
  • Priorities. Every account of the model enters every ordering; there are no accounts that are only monitored.
  • Economic block. It is one goal: every sector has the same direction, and the goal vector (f by default) is the same in every scenario.
  • Corridor. It bounds only the deviations of the economic goals, as proportions of |g_h|. There is no corridor on the output x and no corridor in absolute values.

9. Questions

Can I use one or two satellite accounts? Yes. With k = 1 there is one run per scenario; with k = 2, two.

My satellite accounts are already coefficients. Do I need the levels? No: declare D = instead of E = (and A = or B = instead of Z =).

My vectors are already in R. Do I need to write files? No: pass them to declare_io() by name. write_io() is only for saving the declared database.

Can I run a single priority ordering? Yes: list it in priorities, for instance priorities: {mine: [GC, GD, LAB]}.

Can I run without a corridor? Yes: declare no corridor, or set corridor: use: false in the model or in a scenario.

What does a “not optimal” run mean? That GLPK did not certify some level. Usually it is a numerical false infeasibility, and the numbers are kept; if the level has no solution, it is left blank. See sections 7.1 and 7.5.

How was the package tested? The tests in tests/testthat cover synthetic databases with 2 to 100 sectors and 1 to 5 accounts (dimensions, non-degradation of the higher priorities, invariance to the order of the sectors, to the order of declaration and to the form of the declaration), the corridor modes, the forms of the priorities, the relative deviations, the lock, the outputs, the Miller and Blair example and a comparison of every level with an independent implementation solved with lpSolve.
